summary: Describes how to connect pseudowires across packet network domains or control plane domains, which may be in different autonomous systems or use different protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6073 defines how to join several pseudowire segments into one end-to-end service. Switching PE routers connect the segments and can translate between MPLS and L2TPv3 signaling.

questions: what is an s-pe in pseudowires
how does vccv work on multi-segment pseudowires
subtitle: How switching PE routers connect pseudowire segments across different network and control-plane domains.

tldr.problem: Two pseudowire endpoints may not have direct reachability or may use different packet-network or signaling technologies, so one end-to-end pseudowire cannot be set up directly.
tldr.mechanism: A multi-segment pseudowire joins two or more segments at switching PEs. The switching PE relays setup information, swaps labels for MPLS segments, or maps signaling and encapsulation between MPLS and L2TPv3.
tldr.outcome: The endpoints can provide one point-to-point pseudowire service across multiple segments. RFC 6073 also defines path checks, switching-point information, and status handling; it was updated by RFC 6723 and RFC 7267.

today: RFC 6073 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6723 and RFC 7267. Read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why Segment a Pseudowire
sections.content:
A single-segment pseudowire (SS-PW) is set up directly between two terminating provider-edge routers (T-PEs). That requires the endpoints to know and reach each other's addresses, which may not be possible or desirable across provider or control-plane boundaries.

A multi-segment pseudowire (MS-PW) consists of two or more contiguous segments that act as one point-to-point pseudowire. It can cross distinct packet-switched network domains or use different control-plane protocols. Segments are not independent: the service is instantiated across the complete MS-PW, so setup and operation depend on the full path.

The RFC gives examples involving separate providers, externally computed paths, and hierarchical networks. It does not define path selection or automatic discovery of switching points.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire may need to cross networks whose endpoints cannot set up one direct connection. This RFC joins multiple segments into a single service between the terminating PEs.

sections.title: Terminating and Switching PEs
sections.content:
A T-PE binds a customer-facing attachment circuit to a pseudowire and appears at each end of an MS-PW. A switching PE (S-PE) switches the control and data planes between the preceding and succeeding segments and terminates the packet-switched network tunnels for both.

Setup starts at the T-PEs. The S-PE is configured to connect one segment to another, then relays received setup information to form the next segment's setup message. Multiple S-PEs may occur along the path, and the endpoints do not need to know their number.

Segments use the same pseudowire type. Their transport tunnels may use different technologies; if they do, the S-PE adapts the packet encapsulation. If both segments use the same technology, the S-PE can switch packets at the pseudowire label level without modifying the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: T-PEs attach the customer service at the ends, while S-PEs join the segments in between. An S-PE passes setup messages onward and adapts packet encapsulation when adjacent segments use different transport technologies.

sections.title: Switching MPLS Pseudowires
sections.content:
When both segments use MPLS, the S-PE switches packets with a standard MPLS label swap. When it pushes a new packet-switched network label, the TTL should be set to 255 or another locally configured fixed value. An MS-PW is UP only when every constituent single-segment pseudowire is UP.

For two dynamic LDP control planes of the same FEC type, the S-PE should initially be passive and wait for a remote label mapping before advertising its own mapping. When an MS-PW uses generalized FEC 129 and its path is not statically configured, one T-PE must initiate signaling and the other must wait. Unless manual provisioning overrides it, the T-PE with the larger unsigned SAII assumes the active role.

The PW Switching Point PE TLV (SP-PE TLV) records switching points for management and troubleshooting. Each S-PE appends its TLV and preserves the order. A switching PE should check whether its own IP address already appears in the TLV and report a loop if so.
sections.plainLanguage: For MPLS-to-MPLS segments, the S-PE swaps labels and relays signaling. The SP-PE TLV can record which switching points the path crossed and help detect a repeated point.

sections.title: Recording the Switching Points
sections.content:
The SP-PE TLV is optional to send, but a PE or S-PE must process it when received. Its U bit must be set for compatibility with T-PEs that do not support these extensions. A message may contain one SP-PE TLV for each switching point, and each S-PE appends its own information while preserving order.

The TLV can include the PW identifier of the last segment, a UTF-8 description of up to 80 characters, local or remote IP addresses, the last segment's FEC, and an L2 pseudowire address. Some fields apply only to a particular LDP FEC type.

Most interface parameters pass unchanged through the S-PE. The interface description may be changed or removed, a fragmentation indicator may be added when supported, and the VCCV parameter is reset to reflect the switching PE's supported types. The Group ID has local significance and must be mapped to a unique value allocated by the S-PE.
sections.plainLanguage: The SP-PE TLV records the switching points and segment details for troubleshooting. Each S-PE can add its information, while adjusting the VCCV capabilities to match its own support.

sections.title: Switching Between MPLS and L2TPv3
sections.content:
An S-PE can connect an MPLS pseudowire to an L2TPv3 pseudowire. Between two dynamic segments, the S-PE begins passively and maps an L2TPv3 connection request to an LDP label mapping, or maps a label mapping to L2TPv3 setup messages. Teardown and status messages are translated between the protocols.

Some LDP interface parameters map to L2TPv3 AVPs, including interface MTU, pseudowire type, PWid, and generalized FEC identifiers. Other parameter mappings are unsupported. The SP-PE TLV can be carried in an L2TPv3 AVP of Attribute Type 101, which must not be marked Mandatory.

The S-PE replaces the MPLS label stack with L2TPv3 and IP headers, or the reverse. Sequence numbers have different meanings in the two control-word formats, so transparent forwarding of the sequence number may not work. If sequence interworking is unavailable and requested, the S-PE should refuse the session with result code 31.
sections.plainLanguage: An S-PE translates setup, status, and teardown messages when one segment uses MPLS and another uses L2TPv3. It also replaces the outer encapsulation as packets cross between the segments.

sections.title: Checking the Path with VCCV
sections.content:
VCCV checks can test an entire MS-PW, a contiguous subset of its segments, or the path recorded in the SP-PE TLVs. An optional path-trace operation discovers the data path using FECs returned in echo replies. Path verification uses signaled switching-point information; path trace can also be used with statically configured MS-PWs.

For MPLS segments, each S-PE decreases the PW label TTL as it switches the packet. The sender can set the TTL so the check reaches a particular S-PE. An S-PE replies with return code 8; the egress T-PE replies with return code 3. If the trace receives no reply or an error, it stops and sends no further packets along the MS-PW.

VCCV is specific to the MPLS data plane. At an MPLS-to-L2TPv3 S-PE, MPLS VCCV is terminated and the S-PE must not advertise the VCCV parameter for the L2TPv3 segment.
sections.plainLanguage: VCCV can check all segments or stop at a chosen switching PE. Each reply identifies whether it came from a switching point or the final T-PE.

sections.title: Protecting Data and Control Messages
sections.content:
The data-plane security considerations for the base pseudowire and L2TPv3 specifications also apply. With VCCV Type 3 and no control word, a packet with an unsuitable TTL or mishandled TTL could be forwarded toward the attachment circuit. Enabling the control word prevents a VCCV packet from being forwarded there.

A PE must not accept a session request unless its source address belongs to an eligible peer. The eligible peers may be configured or learned through a trusted discovery protocol, and the network must prevent source-address spoofing. LDP authentication or L2TPv3 control-message authentication may provide message integrity and authentication; both rely on pre-shared keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Only known peers should be able to request a pseudowire, and their addresses must be protected from spoofing. A control word also prevents certain VCCV checks from reaching the customer attachment circuit.
